EMI is a major challenge in electronic device manufacturing.
The literature on EMI and EMC is scattered and not well-organized.
EMI measurement techniques include emission testing and immunity testing.
Radiated emission testing is typically done in an anechoic chamber or a GTEM cell.
Conducted emission testing is typically done using a LISN or a TEM cell.
A reverberation chamber is a type of electromagnetic test chamber that uses a metallic enclosure with a high quality factor.
A GTEM cell is a type of electromagnetic test chamber that uses a tapered two-conductor transmission line.
The frequency range of radiated emission testing is typically 30 MHz to 1 GHz.
The typical distance between the EUT and the receiving antenna in radiated emission testing is 3 m or 10 m.
A LISN is used to stabilize the impedance of the EUT and to measure the conducted emissions.
A TEM cell typically operates from 0 Hz to several MHz.
A reverberation chamber provides more accurate and reliable results in a shorter span of time.
A stirrer is used to modify the boundary conditions of the chamber and to create a statistically homogeneous electric field.
The purpose of EMI measurement is to estimate a device's immunity to unwanted electromagnetic signals and to determine the amount of interference it can generate in its environment.
The two main categories of EMI sources are natural sources and man-made sources.
The two main types of EMI testing are emission testing and immunity testing.
